_comment: G0's P3: which channel carries a frame's worth of bytes from the host to
the content, and at what cost. It is a separate record from both the
capability probe and the performance probe, and the reason is the shape of
the answer rather than tidiness.
The capability record answers with a state and a sentence: SharedArrayBuffer
constructs or it does not. This is a distribution. Putting a distribution in
an `answer` object would make `state` mean 'a measurement happened', which
is the shape that lets a number nobody looked at read as a finding.
The performance record cannot hold it either: its required fields are
input_to_present_p50/p95/p99, missed_vsync_ratio, gpu_bytes -- a renderer's
numbers. P3 runs before any renderer exists; it is what narrows the
transport the renderer will be built on. A record that had to fill those
fields would fill them with zeros, and a zero in a latency field is a lie
with a schema's endorsement.
WHAT A SAMPLE IS. One round trip: the page hands N bytes to the transport
and the same N bytes come back. The echo is the whole of it -- no parsing,
no rendering, no acknowledgement protocol -- so what is measured is the
channel and not what either end does with it.
WHY MEAN AND PERCENTILES ARE REPORTED SEPARATELY, AND WHY ONE CAN BE NULL.
Measured 2026-09-10 on iPhone 12 / iOS 17.0.3: `performance.now()` steps by
0.020 ms on the loopback origin, which is cross-origin isolated, and by
1.000 ms on the custom scheme, which is not. A round trip that takes a few
hundred microseconds is therefore unmeasurable per-sample on the custom
scheme -- every sample reads 0 ms or 1 ms. The mean survives, because a
batch of a thousand round trips takes hundreds of milliseconds and the
quantisation is a rounding error on the total. The percentiles do not, and
the honest record says so with null rather than reporting the shape of the
clock as the shape of the transport.
That asymmetry is itself an input to the architecture: a page that needs to
see its own frame pacing needs a fine clock, and a fine clock needs
cross-origin isolation, which the custom scheme does not have.

_simulator_comment: The simulator runs the host's networking stack on the host's CPU over a
loopback that never leaves it. Its numbers are a Mac's numbers.
The clock asymmetry above, though, reproduces on the simulator -- measured
0.020 ms against 1.000 ms there too -- which is what says it is a property
of cross-origin isolation and not of the phone.
_min_samples_comment: Enough that a 1 ms clock's quantisation is below a percent of the batch
total for any transport that could plausibly be chosen. Below this the
mean stops being trustworthy on the coarse-clock origin, and a mean that
is trustworthy on one arm and not on the other cannot be compared.
_payload_comment: Four of these span what the lane has to carry: an input event (64 B), a
small command batch (4 KiB), a frame's worth of draw commands (64 KiB),
and a texture upload (1 MiB). A transport that wins at 64 bytes and loses
The other three exist to locate a number the implementation needs. The
first run with four classes measured a crossover -- the loopback socket
cheaper below, the custom-scheme request cheaper above, on BOTH latency
and host CPU -- but it could only say the crossover lay somewhere between
64 KiB and 1 MiB, which is a factor of sixteen. A hybrid transport has to
switch at a size, and 'somewhere in a 16x range' is not a size.

_host_cost_comment: A32's threshold has two halves -- "合计 CPU 5% 或 p99 0.25 ms" -- and latency
is only one of them. `host_cpu_ms` and `host_wakeups` are the other, read
from this process's Mach counters around each batch.
They matter because the two channels have different SHAPES of cost. A
WebSocket is one connection and a message's framing per call; a
custom-scheme request is a task constructed, dispatched and torn down per
call. At sixty calls a second the second shape can lose on CPU while
looking level on latency, which is what A32 says to check before declaring
🔴 THIS IS THE HOST'S HALF AND NOT THE WHOLE. The page's own work -- the
JavaScript, WebKit's framing, the response buffer -- happens in the
WebContent process, and iOS gives an app no public way to read another
process's CPU. So these numbers say what the host spends serving a
transport, which is what A32 asks, and say nothing about what WebContent
spends using it. Reporting them as a total would be the measurement
claiming a reach it does not have.
Nullable, and null is not zero: a batch that spent nothing and a counter
that could not be read are different answers.
_host_build_comment: WHY THE HOST'S BUILD CONFIGURATION IS A REQUIRED FIELD.
Half of what these numbers measure is the host's own code. The loopback
arm's server is a WebSocket implementation in this repository -- it parses
frames and unmasks every byte the page sends -- while the custom-scheme
arm's server is WebKit's machinery plus a copy. A debug build of the first
against a release build of the second is not a comparison of transports.
Measured 2026-09-10 on a simulator with a DEBUG host: 1 MiB round-tripped
in 252 ms over the loopback WebSocket and 6.4 ms over the custom scheme.
Four megabytes a second is not a socket's speed; it is an unoptimised
unmasking loop's. That number would have eliminated an arm.
So the configuration is recorded, and a comparison across two of them is
not a comparison. It is required rather than optional because a missing
field reads as `release` to anyone hoping it does.

_nullable_comment: Null where the origin's clock cannot resolve a single round trip. Null is
not zero and it is not a failure: it is the measurement declining to
report a number it did not take.
